speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Conservative senators put off consideration of Bill C-86, a bill to provide over 66,000 Canadian families with pre-payment of the child tax credit before Christmas. The Liberal Senators offered to speed up passage of Bill C-86. The Senate Committee on Social Affairs was standing by ready to receive it, with the intention of passing it by the end of the day. Instead, the Conservative senators said they did not have their notes. They did not know enough about a bill that is only one page in length.
Why did the government not provide notes to its colleagues in the other place? Why did it not explain to the Tory majority that Bill C-86 requires urgent attention, that it was promised by the Minister of Finance back in February? Could it be that Bill C-86 is just another broken promise typical of this government?
Or, is it possible that the newly invigorated "Gang of Eight", enthused by their recent victory in inflicting the clawback and UI cuts on Canadians, want nothing to do with a progressive piece of legislation that could authorize the pre-payment of child tax credits to some of Canada's poorest families just before Christmas?

Mr. Speaker, on October 26, I had the honour of announcing, on behalf
of the Hon. Marcel Danis, that a co-operative education project will start at the Saint-Jerome CEGEP.
The co-operative education option offers students a chance to combine studies with job experience, thus making them better prepared to enter the labour market. Thanks to a federal contribution of $200,000, the Saint-Jerome CEGEP will be able to add a co-operative education component in its curriculum. The CEGEP, in co-operation with business, will then be able to give students the tools they need to enter the labour market successfully.
The Saint-Jerome CEGEP is to be commended for its involvement in the community, and I wish those students who take advantage of the co-operative education option every success.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, when it comes to backing its rhetoric on the environment with solid action, this government's record is sorely lacking.
A case in point is the decision by Canadian National to transport more than 2,000 tonnes of potentially contaminated soil from an industrial site in Halifax, 300 kilometres to River Denys in Cape Breton, rather than carry out the tests necessary to verify its acceptability at a local landfill site.
No, it seems CN could not be bothered to take the time. Nor could it be bothered to consult with the municipality of Inverness, not to mention with the local residents of River Denys. It was easier to find some private landfill operator who would not ask too many questions and then sneak the stuff in, hoping no one would notice. Out of sight, out of mind.
Well, it is not out of the minds of the residents of River Denys who are furious at the prospect of their drinking water being contaminated by the run-off from these materials. Nor to the municipality of Inverness which has

November 7, 1990
had enough problems already with controversial landfill sites, and has had to serve an injunction to stop CN.
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians know how sensitive the disposal of hazardous wastes has become. No community wants to be a dumping ground for some corporation's garbage imported from somewhere else. Certainly, it should not have to be without prior consultation and not by a national Crown corporation on the tacit approval of federal and provincial governments.
CN's behaviour in this case tarnishes its public image and, worse still, erodes the credibility of all governments in the difficult dialogue with citizens over the appropriate disposal of industrial waste.

Mr. Speaker, it is not often that a Canadian member of Parliament has a chance to congratulate a United States governor-she will probably never hear it anyway-but I want to salute Texas Democrat Ann Richards on becoming the first woman governor in the history of the Lone Star State last night.
Now, I would probably disagree with Governor-elect Richards on some issues. But in one respect, her triumph over her Republican opponent, Clayton Williams, is a victory for women everywhere.
Not only did she have her share of discouragements in life; she persevered and came through in the face of Mr. Williams' rudeness, and particularly his unfortunate and shameful gaffe about women and rape.
My wife, Priscilla, and I were cheering on Ann Richards last night. While I know that men are not allowed to wear hats in this Chamber, if I could I would give a tip of my stetson to the first woman governor of the Lone Star State of Texas. Ya-hoo.

It is time once again for our corporate welfare bum of the week award. Today, we would like to present a special effects award to the Liberal Party of Canada for its illusory contribution to the tax system. Its latest concept is a Working Group on Fair Taxation.
The Liberal Party deserves special consideration because it has come up with such an impressive lineup for its committee. Its smoke and mirrors panel consists of
such enlightened corporations as Peat Marwick which in 1988 contributed over $54,000 to both the Liberal and Conservative parties, and Coopers Lybrand which in 1988 donated over $62,000 to the Tories and $52,000 to the Liberals.
These corporate tax experts will no doubt help the Liberal Party keep in place the tax loopholes it put in place while it was in office.
We congratulate the Liberal Party for its portrayal of concern in trying to appear sincere about keeping the average Canadian in mind with its tax committee. There is no doubt in my mind that this group deserves our special effects award for the corporate welfare bum of the week.

subtopic: CITIZENS' FORUM ON THE FUTURE OF CANADA
CITIZENS' FORUM ON THE FUTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and its 170,000 business members have publicly stated their support for the Citizens Forum on the Future of Canada, as announced by our Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, the president of the Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Tim Reid, also mentioned his satisfaction with the Prime Minister's comments regarding the need for putting our financial house in order, if we are to ensure Canada's prosperity during the 90s, and with his awareness of the need to reassess the roles to be played by governments and the private sector in the next few decades, if Canada is to succeed in the international arena.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Reid concluded his press release with a show of support, on behalf of the 500 local chambers of commerce and boards of trade, for the commission and its task to find out what Canadians think about the future of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Fort Petrie as well as Fire Command Post and South Bar Battery are abandoned Second World War fortification sites that have been the subject of great debate in my constituency. I had hoped that government funding for the restoration of these sites would have



November 7, 1990

been made available. However, there does not appear to be any financial assistance forthcoming. Because of the danger and possible safety risks for residents in this area, I must concur with the Municipality of the County of Cape Breton to have demolition commence as soon as possible.
I am certain the historical societies that have worked very hard at trying to secure funding for a restoration project will be very disappointed at this decision.
We must keep in mind, however, that the safety of residents must always take priority. We must secure a safe and secure community, especially for our children who live near these sights.
With this in mind, I urge the Minister of National Defence to commence with the necessary arrangements. I have toured these sights. I have met with the residents and, because there is no financial assistance, I urge the ministry to proceed with demolition expeditiously.

Mr. Speaker, as we approach Remembrance Day, Canadians are facing a challenge of forging a truer understanding of and a greater love for one another and our country. It is most appropriate at this time that we remember those who fought and died so that we would have the freedom to take up this challenge.
While in many parts of the world there is conflict and oppression, in Canada we have the freedom to express our hopes and dreams as well as our concerns. This is a precious gift that we must appreciate and treasure.
On November 11, as we remember the men and women who fought and died in the service of our country, let us also permit the day to be a reminder of the need to show tolerance and understanding to all the peoples of the world.
Let us work together to find greater peace and harmony at home and throughout the world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Minister of Indian Affairs, the hon. Tom Siddon, agreed to start discussions with the negotiating team in Kanesatake, which will consist largely of representatives of a coalition of factions supported by over 400 adult members of the band at Kanesatake. TTie minister also asked for the band council to be represented on the team.
Around the negotiating table will also sit representatives of the federal and provincial governments and of the municipality, parish and village of Oka.
Mr. Speaker, these arrangements are a good start towards dealing with the thorny question of transferring the 97 acres purchased during the crisis and negotiating a single, undivided territory for the people of Kanesatake. I hope the process will be open to the entire Indian and White population in my region, and I trust these negotiations will result in a final treaty between the two communities. I therefore urge all those who wish to take part in this exercise to do so in a spirit of bringing peace and prosperity back to this magnificent and unique area, Oka-Kanesatake.
Finally, I wish Mr. Bernard Roy, who will preside over the negotiations, every success.

Mr. Speaker, the Reform Party is waiy and skeptical as to whether the Prime Minister has learned his lesson on constitutional affairs as far as his penchant for top-down, backroom manipulation is concerned.
Reformers are advocating a bottom-up, people-directed approach to constitution making, rather than the elitist or public relations approaches traditionally employed.
Reformers would prefer a series of constitutional conventions in each region, as well as by aboriginal people, at which delegates directly elected by the Canadian people and assisted by technical experts would

November 7, 1990
debate and vote upon proposals for constitutional changes. The output of these conventions would then go to the traditional parliamentary and legislative processes for review and implementation.
Canadian citizens are concerned about and capable of ensuring that Canada enter the 21st century on sound constitutional footings. All Reformers ask is that Parliament trust the common sense of the common people and let Parliament get on with getting Canada's fiscal house in order.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's first snowfall did not cool the electoral ardour of Jean Chretien. Mr. Chretien's recent statements indicate that he is prepared to fight, and I quote, "against the Mulroney government's right wing corporate agenda."
Will the road to Beausejour be Jean Chretien's road to Damascus?
Canadians, and especially voters in Beausejour, may have their doubts about this miraculous conversion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two nights ago co-operation among all members in this House allowed for the passage of the child tax credit bill. This bill will provide additional assistance for some
70,000	families, representing over 230,000 children.
On behalf of those recipients I commend the members of all parties in the House for recognizing the need for this bill.
However, right now there is another rebate for the same families awaiting passage in the Senate. The goods and services tax is designed to recognize not only children but includes 9 million Canadians living on low incomes. It could provide all of them with money that they need and deserve before Christmas but to do so it must receive immediate passage in the Senate.
I commend those senators who are attempting to do so.
November 7, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Today, Statistics Canada reported that between September and October its help wanted index, a measure of the jobs available across Canada, fell by 3.5 per cent in Quebec, 8.9 per cent in the prairies, 13.7 per cent in Ontario, 16.8 per cent in British Columbia, and 17.1 per cent in Atlantic Canada. That means there are fewer and fewer job openings for the thousands of people losing their jobs now due to the recession induced by this government's policies.
Will the Prime Minister look at his help wanted index and start doing something meaningful right now for the thousands of Canadians who desperately want help to get out of the recession his policies have created?

Mr. Speaker, no one is denying the significance of those figures; they are of concern.
I also say to my hon. friend that we have had a significant increase in employment over the past six years, which has led to a very high level in that particular index. I would caution him about reading too much into that particular index.
Having said that, we recognize the problems in the economy. We have been working to get interest rates down. These, as I pointed out to the House, have come down 1.5 percentage points since the early part of the summer. If the same conditions that brought that about continue, then we can see some further progress in that regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, economic experts have said that what the minister is talking about on interest rates is something that is too little and too late.
Yesterday, the government finally admitted that it has spent more than $400,000 of taxpayers' money on polls to find out something it should already know, and that is, Canadians do not want its GST. Surely the government is not going to spend another $400,000 on still more polls to confirm that we are in a recession and that thousands of
Oral Questions
Canadians and their families are being severely damaged by this government's policies.
Will the government stop wasting money on polls that simply confirm how unpopular and wrong its economic policies are and start doing something meaningful for real people, workers, farmers, and small business people who are being hit hard by this government's misguided economic policies?

Mr. Speaker, there is no surprise at what the poll results are showing. This has been quite apparent for some while now.
I ask my hon. friend, if five royal commissions and task forces of experts that have looked at the existing sales tax say it must be changed, are we as a government supposed to ignore that?
Are we supposed to ignore what Jean Chretien said in 1977 when he pointed out that the existing sales tax was causing our exports to have an additional burden on their backs when they go into the export markets?
Are we supposed to ignore what Allan MacEachen did in 1981, when he was sitting right here in this House of Commons and brought forward a budget which proposed a change in the existing sales tax system?
Are we supposed to ignore the Senate finance committee, dominated by the likes of Allan MacEachen, Michael Kirby, and Sid Buchwold?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Jean Chretien and the Liberals are speaking for Canadians when they say the GST has to be stopped. If the minister is interested in listening to Canadians, he will listen to Jean Chretien and the Liberals who are saying in this House, across the country and in the Senate that the GST must be stopped.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Liberal senators, in accordance with policies announced by Jean Chretien and the Liberals, voted in favour of an amendment that would exempt books and periodicals from the goods and services tax. However, the Conservative senators rejected this amendment. My question to the Prime Minister is this: why does he claim to be listening to the country when he refuses to withdraw his GST and has the nerve

Oral Questions
to tax books? Why does he want to impose his GST? Why does he want to impose ignorance on this country?

Mr. Speaker, Jean Chretien is not leading; he is following Allan MacEachen. I only take that from the media where I see Allan MacEachen saying that he advises Mr. Chretien after he has taken the decision.
The difference is that this government is leading. This government is recognizing the problems of the existing federal sales tax and is moving to remove it.
This government is leading when it recognizes the problem of inflation and takes decisions in advance of the inflation problem getting out of control. This government is leading when it takes decisions to deal with the deficit about which the hon. member opposite, when he was a finance critic for the Liberal Party, asked: "Why are the Conservatives preoccupied with the deficit?"
I will tell him why we are preoccupied with the deficit. It is because of the mess the Liberal Party left this country in. Because it was not preoccupied with the deficit, it is causing the problems that we are having to deal with today.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Yesterday, the minister said that his department ensured that all available information was disclosed to volunteers for clinical testing.
However, the minister is aware that Daniel Trottier, one of the guinea pigs, was never informed that HI-6 could cause birth defects and cancer.
I therefore want to ask the minister to explain how he can say his government's decision to warn future volunteers is a prudent one, when he knows perfectly well that the people who already participated in the tests, like Mr. Trottier, who is watching you today, did not have access to all available information.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not only was the gentleman in question entitled to all the information available, but he signed a form indicating that it had been made available to him and indicating as well the following:
I have read and understood the information about the study and about HI-6 provided in the following pages. I have been informed about the nature and the purpose of the procedures, the benefits and risks that are involved in their performance, and the risks and potential side-effects associated with taking HI-6.1 understand that it is my responsibility to ask questions to clarify any points which I do not clearly understand. I have asked all such questions of the doctor and have received answers to my satisfaction and I understand that I may withdraw my consent and cease participation at any time, without affecting my right to medical care-
The hon. member, if she has bothered to read the consent form as well, will be aware of the fact that the consent form speaks of potential side-effects of the drug. In addition to that it says that as with any drug unexpected and potentially serious effects, including fatality, are always a possibility.
No mention of cancer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite shout across from their seats: "All you did was mention that this could kill you or have other unexpected serious side-effects; you didn't specifically mention cancer".
In addition to all of this, including our warning of possible fatalities, for phase two of the study we have asked that the consent form specifically make mention of the unlikely possibility that it could be a carcinogen as well.
Every effort is being made and has been made to ensure that all volunteers are fully and completely informed.

Mr. Speaker, to pursue the answer of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, let me say that apparently manufacturing of the HI-6 drug is prohibited in the United States because of danger to employees and to the community.
Could the minister assure Canadians today that HI-6 is safe for testing in humans, or will he admit that the necessary tests for cancer in animals have not yet been done?
If the drug is not safe for Americans, why should it be safe for Canadians?
November 7, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is often the case with Liberal members, the hon. member does not present the facts squarely and openly.
HI-6 is not available for sale in the United States, nor is it available for sale or manufacture in Canada. It is precisely for that reason the drug manufacturers are required to go to the Government of Canada to seek approval.
Hon. members opposite say that it is a test on humans. Of course, before a drug is approved for sale in Canada, it must be tested on human beings as well.
Based on all of the information that we have to date, which includes tests that are done in other jurisdictions, we believe that such tests are safe. We also believe that the important criterion of ensuring informed consent was met, notwithstanding the fact that the hon. member's colleague obviously has not bothered to read the form and was not aware of the fact that the individual in question signed a consent form stating that he was fully aware of all of the side-effects, and had asked any questions which needed to be asked and was satisfied with the results.
This was the individual who is quoted in today's Sun as saying that notwithstanding the fact that he was advised not to drink after taking this, he went out and had a beer immediately afterward and found he was sick. It specifically said on the form that that should not be done.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
Yesterday I was in Montreal, where I visited a garment workshop. Mr. Speaker, even before the Free Trade Agreement with the United States was signed, people said this was a vulnerable sector. They were right. It is true this industry is at risk.
One thing is clear and, that is that this government's economic policies: the high level of the Canadian dollar, interest rates, the GST, and free trade with the United States are making the situation worse. Free trade with Mexico would further aggravate the situation.
Oral Questions
Will the Prime Minister say no to free trade with Mexico, protect jobs in the garment industry in Canada and train people who are out of work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister for International Trade has already commented on the possibility of free trade negotiations with Mexico, but I would like to respond to what the Leader of the New Demcoratic Party said at the beginning, about the garment industry.
I think it is inaccurate to attribute the problems being experienced in the sector to the agreement with the United States, because the prevailing situation in the garment industry, Mr. Speaker, is an international one, and it is affected far more by international trade than by our trading relations with the Americans, in which case we have mechanisms for finding a solution.
I believe it is far too early and in fact totally erroneous to claim there is a connection, especially in the Montreal area, between workers in the garment industry and the free trade agreement, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I direct my supplementary question to the Minister of Finance. While this government continues to say that it is too early to tell about the results of the trade deal, it is not too early for the workers who are laid off every day in every sector across this country.
I would like to raise this issue with the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has said that the GST will be good for Canada because industries suffer from the manufacturers' sales tax. The garment industry did not have a manufacturers' sales tax and yet they will be subject to the GST.
On what grounds did the Minister of Finance decide that the GST should be on this industry which did not have a manufacturers' sales tax in the first place?

Mr. Speaker, there is indirect federal sales tax on everything that we buy today. Whether it is food, whether it is clothes, whether it is shoes, whether it is books, whether it is desks, everything has an element of sales tax in it.

Heating oil.

November 7, 1990
Oral Questions
Yes, there is tax on heating fuels as well.
Haircuts.

Yes, there is tax on haircuts. There is tax on everything that we buy today.
What the hon. member is neglecting is that indirect tax. The royal commissions, the task forces, the industry people who have been coming to successive governments since the middle 1950s, have been telling us to get rid of this tax, to get us on a level playing field so we can compete with the opposition internationally.
Clothing which is imported comes in without any sales tax on it. Clothing that is manufactured here has sales tax on it. It is more difficult for clothing companies which manufacture in Canada to compete with international companies.

My supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. Today Statistics Canada issued the help wanted index, and we find that there were 12 per cent fewer jobs available in October than there were in September. That figure varies across the country and is much higher in some parts of the country.
During the last election the Prime Minister promised jobs, jobs, jobs. The economic policies of this government have lost jobs from free trade, to the high dollar, to the high interest rate. What is the Prime Minister prepared to do about the increasing job loss? What is his government prepared to do to get us out of this recession and put Canadians back to work?

Mr. Speaker, my friend says that I promised jobs, jobs, jobs. Indeed, I did that in the campaign of 1984 and we delivered 1.6 million new jobs, the largest number ever in Canadian history. Since the free trade agreement there has been another 300,000 new jobs created in Canada. Because of new jobs, unemployment has declined from 11.6 per cent in 1984 down to the neighbourhood of 8 per cent today.
My hon. friend is well known as an opponent of any attempt to modernize the economy, including free trade and sales tax changes. My hon. friend has been captured and is transfixed by the protectionists, as discussed in a recent article by a leading financial columnist, "Free trade's enemies are predictably overpaid labour unionists
or fat-cat monopolists. While protectionism gets headlines and votes, Canadians must realize that ranting against free trade is a non-starter. Free trade is a profound historical trend which is as immutable as gravity."

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As the minister is aware, there are efforts under way to organize an unofficial all-party delegation to go to Baghdad to make a case for the release of hostages.
I would like to ask the minister if he could confirm comments he made outside the House yesterday where he indicated that the government would be prepared to provide information on the Canadians presently being detained in Kuwait and Iraq, and also provide assistance and services to the embassy and other agencies of the government.
Could the minister tell us exactly what kind of support and co-operation the government would provide to this effort?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member has been quite precise in his question. This government will not authorize a delegation by representatives of Canada to Baghdad. Individual members of Parliament are free to act as they choose.
When individual members of Parliament travel abroad, they are naturally eligible to have the help of Canadian embassy officials. That would be the case with any Canadian members of Parliament who are in Baghdad.
If members of Parliament require a briefing in their private, unofficial capacities, that briefing will be available, whether they undertake a trip there or anywhere.

The
minister will also be aware that many of the families of Canadian nationals presently being held in Iraq and Kuwait have been cut off from any form of financial support or any form of livelihood.
I wonder if the minister would tell us if the government is considering providing some kind of temporary support by way of income or certainly making available things like telephone services to these families until such
November 7, 1990

time as their spouses or their other relatives are released?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is, of course, an extraordinary circumstance and the government is looking at it in that context. There are no existing provisions that would allow the government to work in that way and naturally we would want, as the House would understand, to be very careful not to establish precedents with regard to any actions that we might take.
Having said that, my colleagues and I are looking to see if there is some way in which we can offer help to those Canadians whose families are unable to leave Iraq or Kuwait. We would do that on an extraordinary basis, if it is possible. I cannot give an undertaking to the House at this moment as to whether or not that is possible.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Housing. As you know, CMHC has recently completed an evaluation of the co-operative housing program. This evaluation was supposed to be completed in August, but this government extended its own deadline and stifled input in the consultation process.
These delaying tactics have left thousands of families on waiting lists and hundreds of resource groups hanging, putting co-op projects on hold until this government gets its act together.
I want to ask the minister this question. Will there be a co-op housing program in 1991 to combat the affordability crisis in this country?

Will there be a co-op housing program, yes or no? [English]

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member and all hon. members of the House are aware, the present co-operative housing program is a five-year program. It was necessary to wait until closer to the end of that five years in order to carry out the evaluation. The evaluation has now been com-
Oral Questions
pleted. It is out for discussion and consultation with all interested people, including members and people in the co-op housing field.
I will be making recommendations to cabinet toward the end of this month or the beginning of this month with respect to where we go from here on a new co-op housing program.

Mr. Speaker, that is what worries us, because every time this minister of housing has gone to cabinet he has come back empty-handed. Worse still, there is nothing for housing.
The evaluation by CMHC is not only misleading and incomplete, but it does not examine viable options which would make the program more economical, such as the refinancing of the pre-1985 co-ops using the indexed mortgage mechanism.
Since co-op groups need about six months to prepare for a project, and since this government has delayed this new program, will the minister at least extend the current program for another year and help those people who need housing in this country?

Mr. Speaker, the current program continues until the end of the year. A good many co-operative housing resource groups have projects which they have been developing and are ongoing. There are a great many projects which are in the mill right at the moment and are ready to go ahead next year.
Once I make recommendations to cabinet at the end of the year, we will see where the program goes from there. But I am very optimistic that there will be a co-op housing program and that the hon. member will be quite happy with it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I want to preface my question by expressing my appreciation, that of my colleagues, and the families of those Canadians who are unable to leave Iraq and

Oral Questions
Kuwait, for his agreement to permit a member of the government caucus to join an all-party delegation to that troubled region.
I listened with care to the comments of the minister with respect to his undertaking, which offered support in respect of briefings in Canada and support from the embassy staff in Baghdad.
I want to ask the minister, specifically, in the fortunate event that Canadians who are now unable to leave are in a position to leave following the return of that mission, whether he is prepared to give serious consideration to providing logistical assistance possibly including chartered aircraft to assist those Canadians in those circumstances?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one has to learn to listen to the questions of the hon. member with particular care. It is not a question of permission to private members of the House of Commons. My colleagues in this caucus are free to act on their own. As I have particular cause to know, many of them regularly exercise that freedom. It is not a question of permission. It would be unfortunate to leave on the record any suggestion that there had been an action taken by me as minister, or by any member of the government, that constitutes any kind of official sanction to a trip that might or might not be undertaken.
The second part of the question, as the hon. member well knows, is hypothetical. If a situation arises that requires my response I will respond.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question for the same minister. The minister is well aware of the fact that earlier this week he indicated that it would not be acceptable to his government for a member of the government caucus to attend, and I welcome the change in that position. That is an important change in position.
I want to ask the minister whether he also recognizes the serious concern, not just of the families of those Canadians who are presently in Iraq and Kuwait, but indeed of many Canadians about the importance of giving sanctions time to work. I want to ask the minister whether he is prepared to undertake to this House, as he has been asked before by many Canadians, to only act in a military context in terms of any kind of a unilateral
military action with the full sanction of the United Nations and only after full parliamentary debate and approval of that action?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has a little identity crisis. He is going to have to ask himself the question whether he wants to take the high ground and stay on it, or try to wring partisan advantage out of a gesture that he intends to have interpreted as a humanitarian gesture.
With regard to the second part of the question, this government is working very actively to try to ensure that action which might have to be taken in the Gulf proceeds under UN auspices. We have played a leading, constructive role. Indeed, through our diplomats in the United Nations, we have been responsible for some of the breakthroughs that have allowed United Nations auspices to cover and to authorize the actions so far. We intend to continue to do that. But we also intend that the actions of Canada and the rest of the nations, the 25 nations, rich and poor, north and south, Muslim and non-Muslim, who are arrayed in a coalition against the invasion of Kuwait, be taken seriously by Saddam Hussein. We do not want signals to be sent that would cause him to believe that there is some easy way for him to stay in Kuwait. We do not want him in Kuwait. We want him out and we want there to be no doubt about our position.
Hear, hear.

speechtext:

We are reassuring that the supply management systems will be able to operate in Canada. We are strengthening Article XI as we committed ourselves to do. We are clarifying it, strengthening it, and ensuring that the supply management industries in Canada will remain intact and will be able to grow and become stronger than they are today.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. In spite of what the minister says, Canadian farmers are very concerned about the concessions the Government has already made in its opening position for the GATT negotiations.

What assurance can the government give Canadian farmers that other support programs will not be sacrificed in the GATT negotiations?

about a more equitable and orderly trading regime for all agriculture throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. The minister has announced that he will consult before making a decision. There is nothing wrong with that. Canadians, like King Canute, the medieval monarch who tried unsuccessfully to order the tides to stop coming in, cannot stop the tides of free trade or reject concomitant reforms like the GST. Mr. Speaker, one of the things that we have tried to do in a range of ways, whether it is consulting with groups through the offices of members of Parliament, meetings that ministers have with different groups across the country, groups that the Prime Minister meets, or through the open-line shows where he can talk directly to Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege relating to the actions of the member of Parliament for Edmonton-Strathcona.
It is my contention that this hon. member has brought this House into disrepute by blatantly ignoring the members' allowances and services manual and the guidelines therein.
The hon. member in a recent householder launched an attack on me personally and on the Reform Party of Canada, ignoring the guidelines. The members' services manual states clearly that free household mailings are "intended to provided members with a means for keeping their constituents informed of the workings of Parliament".
Is it considered "the workings of Parliament" when an hon. member states in a householder on page 5, and I quote:
Perhaps she should spend less of her time running around the
countryside with Mr. Manning, practising politics at the taxpayers'
expense?
For the record, I would just like to say that out of the 87 weekends and weeks since my election to Parliament, I have spent 66 of those weekends in my riding. I would hardly consider that running around the countryside with Mr. Manning.
Is it non-partisan, Mr. Speaker, as the guideline states, that the householder be for an hon. member to use the taxpayers dollars on whole pages of vicious, personal attacks on another hon. member? Is it not a blatant disregard for the rights of an hon. member when another member spends taxpayers' dollars in personal and malicious attacks on the character of the former, or to rant rabidly against the policies of another party?
I know that the Canadian people are fed up with what they perceive to be a waste of money that they send to Ottawa. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, and the House, to consider whether this is not a good example of a waste of taxpayers' money, a violation of my rights as a member of Parliament and the privileges that I have of this House in
Privilege
such a blatant disregard for the guidelines and the members' allowances.
Finally, I will just draw to your attention the note on section F(3) of the members' manual. That note states, and I quote: "Householders which are distributed or otherwise used during an election period and which directly promote or oppose in whole or in part a particular registered party or the election of a particular candidate, come within the definition of election expenses under the Elections Act. The cost of printing and mailing these householders or a portion thereof, depending on what portion directly promotes or opposes, should be reported as election expenses".
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Edmonton-Strathcona has begun his campaigning for the next election, considering he used five entire pages of his householder to attack the Reform Party, Senator Waters and myself.
Mr. Speaker, the note says such partisan material does come within the definition of election expenses under the Elections Act. The cost of printing and mailing should be reported as election expenses. As we all know, an election could be a considerable length of time away. Therefore, because this householder has been sent out long before an election writ, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Edmonton-Strathcona be ordered by this House to have the amount of this householder billed to his next election campaign, if he chooses to run. Taxpayers may be more appreciative, Mr. Speaker, if the member be ordered by this House to pay for the cost of printing and mailing this householder, and to pay that personally.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-85, an act to provide for certain matters respecting official languages, employees' pensions and labour relations in connection with the transfer of certain airports, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to move second reading of this bill which refers to miscellaneous matters related to the transfer of airports to local airport authorities.
This bill will permit negotiations to proceed to effect those transfers and to fulfil the objectives of the government's policy in this matter.
The federal government's airport transfer policy dates back to 1987 when discussions began on the basis of certain broad principles of the terms and conditions for the transfer of federal airports to local interested parties. Supplementary principles to guide the negotiations were approved in May of 1989.
Our objectives from the beginning were to allow the airports to better serve the local community interests; to enhance regional economic development potential; and to permit the national airport system to operate in a more cost-effective and commercial manner.
November 7, 1990

Our aim with this policy is to enhance the efficient, commercial operation of federal airports through a more locally responsive management structure.
I should point out at this time that all of the aviation matters, the public safety, the airport fire and emergency response mechanisms will remain with Transport Canada.
But with local authorities at the controls, airports will be quickly able to respond to changing needs and market forces with innovative ideas.
The flexibility that will be afforded to the local airport authorities will enable them to take advantage of the entrepreneurial opportunities that present themselves, and will help them to directly contribute to regional development initiatives.
In the 1987 policy statement and the supplementary principles of 1989, the government prescribed conditions under which airports would be transferred to local authorities. Two of those conditions are of particular importance, and I would like to emphasize them here today.
First, permanent employees must be offered work by the local airport authorities with pay and benefits comparable to what they received in Transport Canada. It is a fundamental principle of the airport transfer process that the employees be fairly treated by the local airport authorities.
Second, on the financial side, current and forecast net revenue generated by the airport must be guaranteed to the government along with a share of the increased revenue produced by the local airport authority.
Intrinsic to this whole process, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the government has recognized that airport employees must be properly looked after. Airport staff are dedicated and skilled professionals and this bill, along with the principles of the transfer process, will ensure that they are treated fairly and equitably.
Early passage of this bill will greatly contribute to allaying the fears of affected airport site employees by dealing with their major concerns. For example, the proposed legislation would give affected employees a year to decide whether to transfer their federal pension benefits to the new local airport authority pension plan.
Government Orders
Employees' collective agreements would be continued by the legislation until they expire or are replaced. The Canada Labour Code and the mandate of the Canada Labour Relations Board would be applied to deal with labour relations issues at and after the time of transfer.
The airport transfer legislation would also ensure that the local airport authorities continue to provide bilingual services to the public at federal airports.
In all of this, I want to assure the House and emphasize that airports are not being privatized. They are being transferred-and my hon. friend from New Brunswick would do well to talk to the people of Moncton who want a local airport authority, so I think before my hon. friend gets too far down the tangent of being opposed, he ought to check with the people back in the region of Moncton and New Brunswick.

airport authorities. The process is now well-established and the pace of progress is gathering momentum.
I can report to the House that substantive negotiations are well under way with local airport authorities in Montreal, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver. These four local airport authorities have received the federal lease rental formula and financial negotiations have been initiated with each of the authorities. Formal transfer to these local airport authorities in the interested communities could take place as early as mid-1991.
I should point out to the House that there has been a learning curve on this and in the negotiations with the first four interested parties we have learned some things, things not only that we would do differently to improve the process but things that we can tell the local airport authorities they can do, so that we can come to a decision more quickly.
As I said to my hon. friend, there is substantial interest in communities such as Thunder Bay, represented in the House by a Liberal member and New Democratic member, and the city of Moncton represented by a Liberal member, Quebec City which naturally has all the Progressive Conservatives representing it, Windsor which is represented by the Leader of the Opposition, and Winnipeg which unfortunately has substantial representation from the Liberal Party.
This is an important piece of legislation. It is consistent and complementary to our government's desire to bring the national air transportation environment some rationality and some efficiency. We believe that this can best be accomplished by the application of the spirit of competition that resides in the public sector. This is the reasoning behind our proposal at Pearson, to select a competitive contractor to modernize and operate Terminals 1 and 2, the non-air process of the airports in the interest of that particular region.
As I said earlier this month, we see no need for the Government of Canada to be involved in the commercial aspects of running an airport. We are looking at leasing because we want the hammer of the lease rather than selling and that is why we are doing it this way.
Also, this fits in with our impetus to initiate negotiations with the United States to establish a bilateral air agreement which will provide better and more frequent air service and foster economic growth.
My hon. friend, being a citizen of New Brunswick, will know the interests of Moncton in achieving greater operation and greater air routes into the United States from Moncton. My hon. friend from Toronto will know that the members from Winnipeg want better access to Winnipeg and from Winnipeg for Canadian airlines and for the people of Winnipeg. That goes for Edmonton and all of the major cities that want better access. That is why this fits in with our local airport authority initiative.
These changes are all in an effort to stay ahead of the rapid growth in aviation in this country. I would say to the House that none of this diminishes in any way the dedication of Transport Canada to providing a safe and secure transportation system. This is a very strong theme, as I learned when I took over this portfolio and it continues. What we want from the local airport authority is this. We want them to be in an even better position to transfer to the local airport authority the energy of the community, to expand the operations at the airport, the non-air operations, the aircraft maintenance, and the aircraft sales, and the parts.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that is possible with this bill. It turns it over to the local authorities to manage the airport. We feel that with the flexibility they would have vis-a-vis some of the restrictions that we naturally face in government that we will have a better airport system and we will have more growth at the regional airports.
These are a very few brief remarks to introduce the bill. We think it is good legislation which will benefit the communities of Canada that have the major airports and I would urge the House to adopt it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party to respond to Bill C-85 which, as the minister has just said, provides the legal framework for the transfer of the management of airports to local authorities. Since the concept of the transfer of airport management to local authorities is new, it obviously requires some new legislation.
November 7, 1990

This bill cannot be looked at in isolation. Bill C-85 cannot be considered without taking other over-all policies of this government as they relate to all modes of transport, particularly in the air, into consideration. Philosophically speaking, I and my colleagues are quite concerned and opposed to the general transfer of authority that has flowed from this government to provincial governments, and now to municipal governments, and to private industry.
What the minister has to recognize, and what the government must recognize is that there is a transportation network in all modes in this country that is absolutely immense, that touches all parts of the country, all Canadians and therefore requires a national set of standards regarding the implementation of our transportation system.
That is not to suggest that we on this side of the House are opposed to having local municipal councils and local community organizations co-operating more fully with the federal government in promoting their local airports. We are not opposed to that. In fact, we have suggested to the minister, concerning the noise of aircraft at Pearson, which affects my riding, that an ombudsman be appointed. The ombudsman could establish a working committee with the local communities so that their concerns would be heard, and when aircraft are flying overhead at three in the morning, and they call the local complaint number, they would not just get a recording. What kind of rapport is that?
We are not opposed to a greater working relationship with the local communities and the local councils. In fact, we have been on record as suggesting and requesting more of that.
But that does not mean that the only way to strengthen relations is by transferring authority away from the federal government to those communities. The fact of the matter is that working side by side with the federal government is also a possibility, and that the two streams are not incompatible.
Therefore, when looking at Bill C-85 you have to take into account the over-all deregulation policy of this government. What does this government say to Canadians when it comes to the question of deregulation in the transport industry, particularly in the air? The first
Government Orders
thing is: "Don't worry. It is good for the consumer. It is going to mean lower air fares". The reality of today is that not only have those air fares gone up, but they have gone up higher and quicker than the rate of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, if you wanted to go to Vancouver today and were going to go to the travel agency, you would find that the increase on those tickets was higher than the cost of inflation. Not only have they stayed the same, but in terms of proportional increases, deregulation has not been the messiah for reduction of air prices that the government has promised.
The only reductions are for booking well in advance, three, four, five, or six months. We had that too before deregulation, so that is simply a non-starter.
It also said that deregulation is going to bring greater competition and greater diversification. Again, a fallacy. What is the reality today? The reality is that we have a concentration and monopolization in terms of the air industry. Under deregulation, 14 regional carriers have been gobbled up by Air Canada and Canadian. Why? Because those air carriers in the economies of scale have moved into the communities, adopted the squeeze play, lowered their fares, and through economies of scale have been able to sustain themselves. In the meantime, the regional air carriers either have gone belly up, been gobbled up, are on the verge of bankruptcy, or are operating with a terrible bottom line.
That is the reality of the messiah that was supposed to be deregulation in terms of diversifying the industry.
It also said that we are going to provide better service for the regions. Once again, look at the facts. Look in your own backyard of western Canada, Mr. Speaker. Look at what my colleagues have been saying in the House from Atlantic Canada. Look at what my colleague, the hon. member for Western Arctic, has said from northern Canada in terms of jet service.
Jet service has been abandoned in many regional centres across Canada. We have had regional jet service removed and put onto the more popular runs. Not only has there been a reduction in service, but the quality has suffered. The quality of service is a bottom line of government. It may not be a bottom line of private enterprise, but it is a bottom line of governments and this institution.

Government Orders
What about safety of aircraft and safety at our airports? Both in the United States and here at home, since the dawning of deregulation the experience has been that safety on both fronts has suffered because some of those companies in the airline industry have cut comers and have been allowed to cut comers. That is of concern not only, of course, to this side of the Elouse, but to Canadians in general.
What about job security under the advent of deregulation? I remember when the minister announced the movement to privatize Terminals 1 and 2. He said this in the context of a larger quote, I admit. One of the things he said is: "I am not in the business of saving jobs." I have news for this minister. Every minister is in the business of saving jobs. They are in the business of promoting, increasing, and developing new jobs to be sure, but he is, and they are also, as part of the government, in the business of trying to save those jobs that we have today.
We know the miserable state of affairs generically speaking, particularly in the transport sector. We have seen the situation in Air Canada, almost 3,000 employees. We have seen it in Worldways. We have seen it in CN Route. We have seen it in the train industry with the VIA cuts.
There is also a quote of July 16, 1985 of the hon. Deputy Prime Minister, the member from Alberta, who suggested: "The government will monitor the effects of change on employees and will try to respond to any adverse consequences as humanely as possible." This was a quote in response to the privatization of Air Canada.
Where is the humane response to the first 3,000 people who have been unemployed as a result of Air Canada tightening its own seat-belts? This may be the first shoe to drop. Where is the humane response? There is none. Therefore, we have one thing being said before its deregulation policy and privatization, and we have a very different reality today.
What about the privatization of Air Canada, not only in terms of the job benefits, but of the investments that people have made? People have lost money on their investment. Air Canada has not been as adamant in
protecting those jobs as it was when it responded to the government.
We cannot only look at Bill C-85 in isolation. We need to take into account deregulation. We need to take into account the privatization concept that has fuelled the privatization of Air Canada? And what about the privatization of airport terminals?
We have in my own city at Pearson Airport a private terminal, Terminal 3. The government has never answered the fundamental question of how does the privatization of Terminal 3 benefit the average taxpayer and the travelling public in the country who are going to be using Terminal 3? More questions have been raised than answers forthcoming from the government.
What about the bidding process for Terminal 3? That is under a dark cloud of many allegations. What about the costs of goods and services in Terminal 3 for the so-called travelling public?
Even the Auditor. General had questions in terms of his last report to Parliament about the privatization of Terminal 3. He stated in his report on page 736, under section 30.84:
The Department should conduct a post-project analysis to identify lessons learned from the Tferminal 3 project. As a minimum, this analysis should address methods for analysing options and safeguards to protect the interests of the Crown.
To protect the interests of the Crown. He goes on to state:
It should form the basis of an improved methodology for handling such private sector developments in future.
I believe that the Auditor General was being very diplomatic and couching his language in terms of some of the things that I am sure will be unearthed in the coming days, weeks and months with regard to the operation of Terminal 3 at Pearson International airport.
Also, what about the moves to greater privatization of Terminals 1 and 2 at Pearson which is the flagship airport. It is the principal airport of our country and basically the hub of all aircraft activity.
What about the 14,000 jobs that are currently at Terminals 1 and 2? Given the general economic outlook of the land, do you not think that these employees are also worried for their security at their job site? Has the minister given any forms of guarantee that those jobs will be protected? Will they be the same guarantees that the
November 7, 1990

government talked about in terms of providing job security for Air Canada employees?
There are many questions that have been raised and many questions that have gone unanswered. The other question with regard to Terminals 1 and 2 is how the government proceeded by putting the cart before the horse? It accepted a number of untendered bids from private firms to privatize Terminals 1 and 2 and then, months after, responded to those bids in a positive way.
Normally, the way governments operate is not do it piece-meal, one airport at a time. They do it on a comprehensive basis if they believe in it. Second, they set the incentives and the parameters for those policies. They do not generally respond to private firms and private interests, allowing them to dictate the policies of the day. Rather, the government, as a national institution, should speak up on behalf of the entire transport industry and the country.
What about the regional services? Does it mean that the less popular runs will be abandoned in terms of jet service to the regions, as I mentioned earlier?
What about the fact that open skies will now be coming? That is another issue which has to be taken into account when we talk about the greater tendency to privatize and to delete the authority from the central government? What about the open skies concept?
We know that the Minister of Transport and the government is prepared to deregulate the 1974 air agreement that exists at the moment between Canada and the United States. Essentially, this amounts to free trade in the sky. We know what the advent of the free trade agreement has brought, in terms of job losses and plant closings. Although Canadians may favour modifying any existing agreement, I do not see the political green light there, as yet, to suggest a complete deregulation of that agreement.
Can we compete under an open skies concept with the United States of America? Does the government recognize that, in terms of air carriers, the Americans have perhaps a dozen major airlines that could compete and we have only two major airlines? Does the government take into account that American Airlines alone has over 500 aircraft, while Air Canada has 104 and Canadian has 90? Our two major airlines combined do not have even
Government Orders
one-third of the air carriers of just one major American airline company.

That is not open skies. That is not on a level playing field. That is a re-regulation of the current agreement, a modification upon conditions, and not a deregulation of the 1974 agreement completely. Industry observers say that Canada's two major airlines may not survive in the face of the United States competition, or at least not in their current form.
Steve Garmaise in the Financial Post, which this government loves to quote day in and day out, an analyst for First Marathon Securities Ltd., has predicted that Air Canada and Canadian Airlines may have to merge international routes within five years if U.S. carriers compete head to head with Canadian air carriers.
Tony Hine, an analyst for ScotiaMcLeod Inc. said that two airlines might have to become feeder services to larger U.S. air carriers. That is on another front called the open skies.
We also have a move to once again privatize user fees on the altar of cost recovery on the basis that the government does not have the necessary capital or perhaps does not attach the necessary priority on having the necessary capital with respect to cost recovery programs.
In the shipping industry the government may in fact, upon consultations that will be completed on February 1, try to raise $25 million through imposing new fees that have never been imposed before on shipping companies which use the services of our national Coast Guard.
Does this government recognize that our shipping industry is one of the greatest success stories in the Canadian transport industry, so much so that the Americans were not willing to compete with us in the shipping industry, and is on a troubled course as it is right now, that shipping has gone down 10 per cent, that jobs have been lost in the shipping industry as well and that any increase in additional fees will only serve to destabilize shipping industries?
When we speak of the interests of Quebec, the Port of Montreal and the Port of Quebec City and the large shipping infrastructure in that province, we are going to impose on the province of Quebec-and I see some colleagues from that province on the opposite side-over half of the $25 million to be raised from the province of Quebec's shipping industry, namely $14 million out of the $25 million in terms of increased costs. What about the cost recovery program in terms of landing rights at our airports across Canada? My colleague from the province of New Brunswick stood in his place today. My colleague from northern Canada, the hon. member for Western Arctic, stood last week. People in our caucus in western Canada suggested that the cost recovery basis in terms of landing fees is simply unfair, inequitable and unworkable. Up to now the landing fees have taken into account that smaller aircraft travel shorter distances, carry fewer passengers and charge less in terms of ticket fares and therefore generate less revenue. Therefore, the landing fees for smaller aircraft take into account those variables.
Now the government is contemplating abandoning those variables and suggesting that the landing fees should be based on only a proportional weight of the incoming aircraft. What will that mean? It will mean two things. First, smaller aircraft will pay proportionately greater amounts to land in the airports than larger aircraft. Second, the regional airports in the regional

hinterlands of Canada will have to pay greater amounts of money because they have the greatest amount of smaller commuter feeder airlines, which means that those costs will be passed on to the travelling public.
It has been estimated that in regions such as Atlantic and western Canada the travelling public will pay upward of 25 per cent more for their tickets of airlines' smaller Dash-8 service as a result of those airlines having to pay greater amounts of dollars to land at the respective airports. For instance, in St. John's the Dash-8 increase will be 32 per cent. In Gander, it will be 12.7 per cent and in Deer Lake, a 57.2 per cent increase in landing fees. Is this the government's idea of equity across the country? Is this the way it will balance the needs and aspirations of Canadians who do not happen to live in the large urban centres? Is that what the government means when it talks of a policy of regionalism? I would suggest that it is an absurd view of this country that not only will not work, but will not be acceptable to and tolerated by Canadian citizens across the country.
It is for those reasons that I am opposed to the general benchmark of decentralization, deregulation and privatization policies of this government. The dreaded DDP, decentralization, deregulation and privatization. They are linked. You cannot look at one without isolating and looking at the others. Therefore, in terms of the specific concerns on Bill C-85, we have a two-track approach; we have to link them with the other policies that have been enunciated and also begin to cross the t,s and dot the i,s in terms of what it means to local authority transferships.
Number one, what about the responsibility of safety and security? We have had the experience under deregulation. Does this mean now that in a transfership to local authorities that the security and safety aspects of all types of transport modes will be sacrificed? If it is, is it worth the price of transferring holus-bolus authority to local communities and local cities? I think not.

If you are an employee and part of a membership of 125 or if you are an employee and part of a membership of 12,000, and someone has to speak for you, which one would you as an employee choose? Obviously, you would choose the larger one because they are interested, unlike members who yell.

I suggest it is not right because those airports are part of a national service. If there is an airport in Edmonton, it is not only Canadians from that city who use that airport. It is Canadians from all over the country. Therefore, that burden must be equally shared.
What about number seven, local authorities having a double standard. That is to say, local authorities would be lining up to get the authority for the very popular often used airports.
What about the less used airports in the north, in the east and in the west? Will authorities rush to try to obtain the authority and power over those airports? If they do not, we are going to have two tiers. We are going
to have local authorities at the popular airports, and the Government of Canada in the other airports.
What is that going to mean in terms of the service for Canadians at all those airports? We obviously are getting into a different bottom line arrangement with this government. Canadians and Liberal members on this side do not like it.
I mention this briefly because I believe I only have about five minutes left in this discourse. I would love to continue. I might if members on the opposite side are so disposed, but I and members in my parity are concerned about the application of the official languages component to Bill C-85.
There is a strong concern whether the federal principle of bilingualism is going to be safeguarded and protected.
The minister will know that the Official Languages Act is divided into 12 parts. In fact, a number of those parts are not entirely interested in terms of local authority. That is why it is obvious that parts I, II, III, VI and VII 7 are not included in Bill C-85. They are not legitimately relevant.
However, it is not so obvious why Part V-Language of Work, Part Vl-Participation of English Speaking and French Speaking Canadians, and Part VH-Advancement of English and French are not included in Bill C-85.
The operative clause in Part V states:
English and French are the languages of work in all federal institutions, and officers and employers of all federal institutions have the right to use either official language in accordance with this Part.
It would seem anomalous to have a Part of Bill C-85 which reports to protect the use of both the French and English languages in relation to the public, if the employee's use of either language is not protected.
Why is Part V of our Official Languages Act not applicable in Bill C-85?
Part VI states:
This Part states that the Government of Canada is committed to ensuring that English and French Speaking Canadians without regard to ethnic origin or first language have equal opportunities to gain employment or advancement in federal institutions. The workforce in particular federal institutions should also reflect the presence of both official language groups.
Again, this is a Part of the Official Languages Act which is designed to protect workers of both groups.

It is not part of Bill C-85. It is difficult for my party and I to understand the rationale behind that glaring omission.
Part VII reads:
This Part states the commitment of the Government of Canada to enhancing the vitality of English and French linguistic minorities in Canada and fostering the full recognition and use of both English and French in Canada.
The task of doing the above is given to the Department of Secretary of State. This department is given the right to encourage and co-operate with the provinces and the public in general to accomplish the mandate given to it by this statute.
We are asking on this side of the House why Part VII is omitted from Bill C-85 and thus the Department of Secretary of State is not permitted by legislation to carry out its mandate under this very important part.
I urge the minister who is present in the Chamber to reconsider the words he spoke earlier. In fact the Official Languages Act is absolutely not protected in three crucial parts of its 12-part mandate. That is not in keeping with the Prime Minister's so-called goals of national reconciliation, of somehow having peace between our linguistic duality, and of increasing the opportunities for all Canadians regardless of their ethnocultural extraction.
In this bill is an abandonment of those principles by virtue that it does not permit three of the twelve parts in our Official Languages Act to govern equality among our linguistic groups, and that is a shame.
In conclusion, we are very distressed on this side of the House that this government has allowed its perverse sense of decentralization as contained in this bill. Deregulation is the messiah of the Tory government for Canadians. Privatization is hurting the transportation industry and is hurting Canadians. It has not improved the transportation industry. It is sinking our shipping industry. It is derailing our trains. It is stopping and stifling our aircraft on the ground.
I have much respect for this minister. I hope that he still has time enough to turn things around. This government is going through some turbulent times. This bill will not improve it. This bill will aggravate it.
We will fight decentralization, deregulation, and privatization with every Canadian fibre that we have.
