speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate on Bill C-85, although I would have preferred to hear my friend and colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace, who today is celebrating 25th anniversary as a member of this House. As you know, Mr. Speaker, today the Hon. Warren Allmand is being honoured in his riding and is therefore unable to be in the House. He asked me to make a few comments on this bill, reserving the right to add further comments later on and perhaps expand on, and further explain, our objections to certain clauses in the bill.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-85 is to provide for certain matters respecting official languages, pension plans and labour relations.

I shall leave my colleagues and friends on the Liberal side of the House to handle questions dealing with the protection of employee benefits, as to whether the government will ensure that employees do not lose their pensions and pension benefits once the local authorities have taken over airport management.
We have to remember that when CN decided to privatize Route Canada all employee benefits and pensions were lost due to mismanagement. I will leave that to some of my colleagues who are much more familiar with the issues.
We have an issue here dealing with the protection of jobs. The government must again ensure that all jobs at local airports are retained once they are under local management. We have in our minds the privatization of Air Canada. We all remember the Deputy Prime Minister in this House assuring us that the jobs would be protected. In October 1990, 2,900 people lost their jobs and had no federal protection. I will also leave to some of my colleagues in the Liberal caucus the obligation to oppose this bill based on what kind of guarantee local
November 7, 1990

Government Orders
taxpayers will have so that they will not be obligated to pick up any deficit that is incurred by the administration of these local airports. Other items or rules such as the six-month protection of employees' jobs, which members will recall is a right of Public Service employees, should in our view apply to the transfer of the airports to regional authorities.
I want to address one very important item in this bill that deals with the official languages. Having spent 10 years as critic for my party on this matter and having been a member of the standing committee since its creation in 1979,1 have a special obligation to make sure that we scrutinize legislation so that it conforms with existing laws and that the government is taken to task if it does not. I want to remind my members that the clause to which I will be addressing my comments is clause 4 of the bill that reads as follows:
Where the Minister has sold, leased or otherwise transferred an airport to a designated airport authority, on and after the transfer date Parts IV, VIII, IX and X of the Official Languages Act apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, to the authority relation to the airport as if
(a)	the authority were a federal institution; and
(b)	the airport were an office or facility of that institution, other than its head or central office.
I know it is complicated, Mr. Speaker. That is why I will take a few minutes, with your indulgence, to explain the impact of this clause, how we feel it should be strengthened, and possibly where the principle is not exactly in keeping with the spirit of the Official Languages Act.
Let me read first of all what the act says. We adopted Bill C-72. It was passed by the House of Commons on July 7, 1988. Section 23 of the act says: "For greater certainty, every federal institution that provides services or makes them available to the travelling public has the duty to ensure that any member of the travelling public can communicate with and obtain those services in either official language from any office or facility of the institution in Canada or elsewhere where there is significant demand for those services in that language."
Mr. Speaker, the government has included a vital clause in Bill C-85. Following the privatization of a number of federal agencies, the government was ordered to make the Official Languages Act binding on the authorities of these newly privatized institutions so that the Canadian public will be able to obtain services in French or English, as the case may be and as the customer, in other words, as Canadian men and women prefer.
Mr. Speaker, under Part IV of the Act the new regional or municipal authority-God only knows what this new commission will be-has a duty to provide services in the language of the customer's choices. Although the language of service is included in the present legislation, we note that the working language- the language used daily by employees-and the principle of equitable participation-in other words-equitable representation of both official language groups in the organization-have been totally ignored. This means that employees at these so-called privatized or restructured airports will no longer have the assurance that they can work in the official language of their choice. It will depend on the good will of local management.
The government has made no provision for ensuring that these new institutions provide for equitable participation of both official language groups. Mr. Speaker, official language minorities will bear the brunt of all this. In Quebec, an airport like Dorval, for instances might be transferred to the private sector. What would happen if the so-called management of this new air terminal commission decided that French was the language of work at headquarters? How can management ensure that employees use both official languages, when management uses only one? We've got a problem, Mr. Speaker!

The central administrative office will be operating in one language because it is excluded by the act. It is not the same; it is not subjected in the same manner to the Official Languages Act. How will that central office which will be using one language-it could be English in Edmonton or franqais a Dorval-encourage its employees to use both official languages when only one language is used at the head office? That is a problem we

November 7, 1990
Government Orders
have addressed for many years in this House. The employee will be obliged to use the language of the administration. If it is French in Dorval, it will be to his or her detriment. If it is anglais a Edmonton, he will have to use the language of the administration. That will be the way the system will operate.
Using that same example, what happens if the travelling public, which by law is entitled to receive services in either language from the new commission, is not satisfied and wants to complain to the administration directly? It cannot do that.
If the language of work of the central administration is other than the travelling person's language, that is if it is French in Dorval or English in Edmonton and the travelling person happens to be from the other language group, he has a heck of a problem because the administration does not speak his language. That again presents us with a certain problem because, as is the case with the employees, the travelling public will be obligated to use the language of the administration. That is a problem which will have to be resolved.
One could say that we will wait before making any decisions on this subject. It has been two and half years since we have adopted this new Official Languages Act, and we have no regulations. We have no definition of what is an institution.

Mr. Speaker, I simply wanted to remind the House of some definitions that are essential to our understanding of the regulations arising from legislation as important as the Official Languages Act.
We have waited two and half years for the government to table these regulations. We still do not have a definition of "significant demand", for instance. We do not have a definition of "office".
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, as you well know, but we are still waiting. And how are we going to tell Canadians that an office is defined as- It could even be a horse, Mr. Speaker! It could be a horse ridden by a policeman who provides a service here at the House of Commons and is obliged to answer Canadian visitors in the language of their choice. In English or en frangais. If a policeman is not capable of answering Canadians who
visit Parliament Hill during the summer- Because that is his office, and he just happens to sit on a horse.
People ask him: sir, what is that statue? where's the washroom? what's that building? Well, if the policeman cannot answer, Mr. Speaker, his office, as I defined it-the definition may be a little farfetched, but it is there just the same-the office is incapable of providing the service.
I am sure hon. members will say: sure, but let us not exaggerate. I want a definition of an office. What constitutes an office? I want a definition of "significant demand".

What is significant demand? How do you define significant demand? These are the things we addressed in committee and in the House two and a half years ago, and the government has yet to give a definition. Yet we have a law before us today that says the Official Languages Act applies in regard to significant demand. Who will determine that?
I will quote the same article which states that the law applies with such modifications as the circumstances require. That is discretionary to the local commissions or boards, whoever it might be and however it be intended to apply the law of the land. If we do not tell the commissions what the laws are, and if we do not tell them what the federal government and this Parliament meant when it passed that law, how the heck are they supposed to do it?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for the information concerning the four members of the House who are celebrating their anniversary. speechtext:
That is right, two more years.
Getting back to Bill C-85, it is described as an act to provide for certain matters respecting official languages, employees' pensions and labour relations in connection with the transfer of certain airports.
I listened to the minister and I congratulate him for having stayed around for the two subsequent speeches, but I really am at somewhat of a loss to understand where in his speech he made any relevant reference, any meaningful reference to the specifics of what is in the bill. I am rather glad that he did not because it gives me an opportunity to make reference to some of the things he talked about although he may have been speaking in a rather oblique way.
The minister talked about efficiency, better service, cost efficiency, entrepreneurship. I see those things relating to privatization, as one of the previous members mentioned.
I see it being referred to as well as deregulation, to which one of the previous speakers referred. He had a third, and I guess it could be referred to as the "pillar", as we have been talking a lot about pillars in connection with the banking industry. I think they could also be referred to as the three pillars of Progressive Conservative philosophy of the last two years since I came into the House, namely, deregulation, privatization and free

November 7, 1990
Government Orders
trade, which is not what the member for York West referred to as a third reference.
When the minister takes a bill such as I read out, and refers to how much better service we are going to have, how cost efficient it is going to be, how it is going to have effective commercial operations and entrepreneurial benefits, he can only be referring to deregulation and privatization. I would suggest these have shown no efficiencies and no great entrepreneurial potential either. Certainly they have not shown better service.
If we refer to deregulation, whether it be of the trucking industry or the airline industry, or even the shipping industry, which is coming about, it certainly is proof that there have not been any of these efficiencies. The potential, which is supposed to be so inherent in what the government is doing with the airports, is not there.
As far as free trade is concerned, the promise of wealth and plenty for this country of ours certainly has not materialized in any way. As a matter of fact, we hear on a daily basis how much of a tragedy the free trade deal with the United States has been for this country. We also hear the fears expressed on a daily basis on how much more tragic this government's policies are going to be for this country when it gets into the free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico as well.
The minister stands up and speaks in such glowing terms of the potential of turning these airports over to local airport authorities. There is no reason why anyone on this side of the House should gain any comfort from what the minister says is going to occur.
There are many other examples of the government bringing forward, in glowing terms, bills it has introduced and saying how the country is supposed to become prosperous because all these wonderful things are going to occur.
One of the things which the bill talks about about is employees' pensions. These are so vital to the federal government employees and must be protected after the employees are transferred to the local airport authorities.
If we look at Bill C-21, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the evidence is certainly there that this government's legislation, proposed in glowing terms, is going to
turn out to be an absolute disaster for the working people of Canada. There is no protection for them within that legislation at all.
As I have already pointed out, there is certainly no protection for the Canadian people within the concept of privatization, deregulation and free trade. Reference was made earlier on how the government is divesting itself of these presumably profitable airports. I suppose you could read along with that, Mr. Speaker, efficient and possibly even cost-effective, and perhaps, even better service in these larger profitable airports.
On the other hand, the smaller ones and I suppose also by implication from what the minister said, perhaps less efficient, where there is not quite as good service, and maybe not quite so much potential for the entrepreneurial potentialities, although what is supposed to be referred to within that I am not entirely sure. Perhaps it is all these little kiosks we see springing up in the airports where entrepreneurs have started up. I suppose, at least theoretically, they are making a tremendous amount of money on these little businesses they have set up.
The logic of it still escapes me. Why the government would not get rid of the inefficient ones which presumably are costing them money and let the real entrepreneurial spirit of this country take over and turn these smaller, less efficient, perhaps even implied because they are government run. Although we certainly have a great deal of experience in Saskatchewan which would prove that government run-particularly New Democratic government run operations-can be tremendously efficient-

-and tremendously profitable. It does escape me why the government would not turn these small airports over to the entrepreneurs and really prove to this country how wonderful the entrepreneurs of this country are.
Instead of that, of course, and I am really begging the question because we know the answer anyway, the government is turning over to their friends in the larger centres the operation of the airports where there is a tremendous amount of potential for making profit.

I am not entirely sure what is going to be done with the profit because the act does say that the "leased, sold or otherwise disposed of" airports. It does not say there could be no private companies, but it does not say it cannot create some kind of a corporation and, presumably, set up directorships and so on. I would suspect there is a lot of potential within that for being able to pay themselves rather handsomely as airport managers and chief executive officers, vice-presidents, and so on of the local airport authority.
I would suspect that as much as anything is what is behind most of this. Otherwise the government would be testing the Canadian entrepreneurial spirit in turning the small airports over.
The small airports will be staying in the hands of the Canadian public who are going to have to shoulder the burden of them running inefficiently, certainly as this government has proved it is able to do.
The minister has referred to the assurance that the aviation safety aspect which we now enjoy and as has been pointed out by one of the previous speakers, is pre-eminent in Canada. One of my colleagues was referring to a pilot from an airline in the United States who said that he would much rather fly on a Canadian carrier across the country than anything else whenever they had the opportunity.
I would suggest that that is something of which we are tremendously proud but I would also suggest that there is a tremendous amount of potential there for us to be losing that safety factor within the Canadian aviation industry.
I would also suggest that the whole matter of safety within the airports themselves, has been alluded to already, is going to suffer enormously. It is bad enough at the present time. There are many times when the Canadian public, if they really knew what was happening on the ground, would probably do the very best they could to avoid flying on those later flights. The evidence is certainly there that there is not a lot of protection when it comes to flying later in the day. Once these airports become privatized, there is every likelihood that that will increase much more.
As far as the workers themselves are concerned, the question again is begged because, as has been pointed out, the unions involved were not consulted. While the government seems to pride itself in saying that it very

seldom does anything such as this, bringing in legislation or making changes within the legislation without consulting the people involved, we know, of course, time after time, that is not the case. This bill is supposed to be about the protection of workers. Those who represent the workers now are not protected.
I would like to conclude by making reference again to the workers, and particularly to their probability maintaining the standard of living and the level of wages and benefit which they now do as employees of the federal government under these local airport authorities. While some of them may possibly be successful, some are not going to be successful. It begs the question: What are we going to do with these once well-paid, well-trained civil servants who will undoubtedly find themselves out of jobs because of the failure of some of the local airport authorities to be able to function in the manner in which the government so erroneously assumes they are going to be able to do?
There has to be some changes made to this legislation for the protection of the workers not just for the short term, but for the long term, over their whole working lives. We have to make sure of the remuneration for these people, and not just the permanent people, as the minister pointed out and as the legislation supposedly points out, although permanent may be the operative word. It may be that, within the whole context of what is about to occur, we are going to find a tremendously larger number of temporary employees in these airports. This is a tragedy, but something which has to be addressed and certainly will be addressed before this legislation comes to a conclusion.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate this opportunity to speak to Bill C-85, even though I have but eight minutes today, unless you are prepared to be friendly and extend the-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

subtopic: AIRPORT TRANSFER (MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Seven minutes? Aren't you kind, Mr. Speaker. I will speak for seven minutes and resume my comments next day.
We on this side of the House are concerned about this piece of legislation. It is one small step in the long journey that the Prime Minister and the Conservative Party embarked upon in 1984 to sell out the country. The Conservative Party and the Prime Minister, starting in 1984 decided to put Canada out of business. In other words, they decided to privatize different federal institutions and different federal Crown corporations in order to satisfy the right wing element of the Conservative Party.
Is it any wonder that Mr. Spicer and others have to travel from one end of the country to the other to deal with national unity when this government six years ago started to pull apart the country? It started to divide the country because of its policies and, in particular, its policy with respect to privatization.
The federal government has a role to play in order to keep this great nation together because, without the federal government and without federal government policies, the only thing that binds Canadians and the only thing that we would have in common is the fact that we share the northern half of North America. It is the only thing we would have in common. What else would a potato farmer in Prince Edward Island and a forest worker in British Columbia have in common?

The government set out in 1985 to dismantle Canada and dismantle the very infrastructure that has kept the country together.
The Prime Minister started by going to New York City to visit with his American friends to indicate to them that the Foreign Investment Review Agency would be eliminated. Canada, in effect, was up for sale and no longer would the Canadian government have the authority to determine what was in the best interests of Canada insofar as foreign investment was concerned.
The message started back then. The message was loud and clear. Since that time we have seen many small steps and many large steps that have led to the disintegration of Canada. Let me just name a few. Air Canada. The government decided to privatize Air Canada. Why? I do not know. Air Canada belonged to the people of Canada. It was one of those crown corporations that kept the country together because through that crown corporation, in a very direct way, the government was able to provide for air transportation to many communities in Canada that today do not have the jet service that existed when Air Canada was a crown corporation.
Petro-Canada. The government now wants to privatize Petro-Canada in order to line the pockets of their rich friends on Bay Street.
Harbourfront in Toronto. Canada Place in Vancouver. Canada Post is on the privatization block now. The unemployment insurance system in Canada is being privatized. Is it any wonder that Canadians are asking themselves today, what does it mean to be a Canadian? Why should we continue to be together when the government is hell bent on destroying the country?
This bill, as innocuous as it may seem to some, as innocuous as it may seem to members on the government side, is another small step. The Government of Canada has decided it does not want to be in the airport business. Why?

the airport business. Toronto International Airport last year netted some $60 million profit, net profit. Where did that money go? It belonged to the people of Canada. That money could have been used to upgrade and subsidize airports in smaller centres across the country. What did the government decide to do? Give it to the private sector.
Is it any wonder that, the construction and management of Terminal 3 was given to the private sector and Huang Danczkay. They are not there to provide a service to the people of Toronto, to ensure Torontonians and others in southern Ontario that they have the opportunity to be part of an efficient transportation system. Huang Danczkay and all the other Tory flaks and businessmen were lining up to run Terminal 3 because there was a significant profit to be made.
The government decided in Bill C-85 to provide for certain matters respecting official languages, blah, blah, blah. We know what all this means. It means the government is privatizing and giving to local authorities the operation of certain airports across the country. Why are we not dealing with that bill first? Canadians do not know at this point. Who are these local authorities in Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary or Montreal? We do not know who these people are. The government is putting the cart before the horse. We should first deal with the issue of privatization.
I see you are on the edge of your seat. You are about to cut me off, but before you do, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I look forward to the opportunity when we meet again on Bill C-85 to continue my comments and to criticize the government for destroying the country.
